summary: The developer can start implementing the FastAPI + Beanie DocumentDB sample against the reachable cluster. All runtime tooling the sample requires (Python, pip, Docker for optional local gateway, and the DocumentDB MCP data-plane server) is present. Authoritative documentation and agent skills exist for the main design decisions (resource type, CLI, connection string, driver patterns, TTL, indexing, vector & full-text search, Entra ID auth). Gaps: some common model answers from the cold run are outdated or conflate Cosmos DB account APIs with the newer DocumentDB mongoClusters resource; mongosh is missing on PATH (handshell checks would benefit), and one known accelerator (DocumentDB Agent Kit) is not present in the inventory and would speed building/verification if added. None of the gaps block building the sample; they increase the chance the builder will use the wrong ARM/CLI resource types or the wrong connection-string options if they rely on the cold answers instead of the docs/skills.
summary_points: Ready to start: Python, pip, Docker, az, node/npx, the documentdb MCP server (connection_profile 'default') and Microsoft Learn 'learn' MCP are all available and sufficient to build and verify the sample.

Several cold answers are incorrect or outdated — most importantly the ARM/CLI resource type and command group (use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and az documentdb mongocluster, not databaseAccounts/az cosmosdb for this offering).
Auth, connection-string format, TTL index semantics, driver choices (Motor + Beanie) and index guidance are verifiable in the installed skills and Microsoft Learn pages.

Missing accelerators and CLI tools: DocumentDB Agent Kit (accelerator) and mongosh (manual shell) are not installed; add mongosh to simplify manual checks; the agent kit would speed sample creation but is not required.
Verdict is ready_with_gaps because all required items exist and nothing essential is unverified, but some cold facts must be corrected and small tooling additions recommended.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the FastAPI service, pip install dependencies, run seed/test scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the Python FastAPI + Beanie sample locally.
tools.workaround: Install Python 3.11+; use Docker image with Python if local install is blocked.

tools.name: pip (via python)
tools.needed_for: Install FastAPI, Beanie, Motor and other Python dependencies.
tools.detail: Assumed available via the Python runtime in the environment.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot install dependencies; cannot run sample.
tools.workaround: Use a virtual environment or Docker image that includes pip.

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect cluster and resource metadata, create temporary firewall rule if required by developer, or to read connection strings from the control plane (if needed).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to read control-plane metadata, but not required to run the sample against an already-provisioned cluster.
tools.workaround: Use the DocumentDB MCP server data-plane tools and the Azure Portal for connection string and firewall settings.

references.title: az documentdb mongocluster commands (Azure Learn CLI docs)

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the DocumentDB local Gateway image for local integration tests.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the DocumentDB local Gateway container; must test against live cluster only.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster reachable via DOCUMENTDB_URI as instructed in the run environment.

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: Install or run MCP helpers or agent skills (npx skills add) and any Node-based build tools if used.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to add MCP skills or run some agent-tooling; not required for the Python sample itself.
tools.workaround: Use installed MCP servers and skills via the inventory; use alternative tooling to install skills.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection: list databases/collections, create indexes, run sample queries, explain plans, insert and update test documents to verify the app-created artifacts.
tools.detail: DocumentDB MCP server present with 18 data-plane tools (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_find_documents, explain, etc.) and requires connection_profile "default" (inventory).
tools.impact_if_missing: Would lose an automated, scriptable data-plane verification path to check indexes/collections and to insert sample data safely; would need to rely on manual Portal/az commands.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI, Azure Portal, or REST APIs; but the documentdb MCP server is the most convenient programmatic verifier.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Search and fetch authoritative Microsoft docs to verify facts and follow official code samples.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to ground cold answers against authoritative documentation inside the agent environment.
tools.workaround: Use web searching outside MCP or rely on installed skills' builtin references; both are inferior.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver best practices (singleton MongoClient, connection pooling) and guidance when writing Beanie/Motor integration code.
tools.impact_if_missing: Increased risk of connection-pool misuse (creating a client per request) and connection exhaustion in the sample.
tools.workaround: Follow Motor/Beanie official docs manually; implement a singleton client pattern.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Index selection and TTL guidance (create TTL index with expireAfterSeconds=0 on expireAt field).
tools.impact_if_missing: Less precise index guidance; sample might create suboptimal or unnecessary indexes.
tools.workaround: Follow Microsoft Learn index docs directly.

tools.name: documentdb-full-text-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the sample later adds text or hybrid search, guidance for createSearchIndexes and $search usage (recommended over community $text).
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of using community text indexes which are not the DocumentDB recommended path.
tools.workaround: Use SQL-level or external search as a fallback; but for this sample text search is optional.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the sample uses vector embeddings or stores vectors, indexing guidance and index creation patterns (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF).
tools.impact_if_missing: If vector features are added, incorrect index choice can hurt latency/recall.
tools.workaround: Keep the sample vector-free, or use documented defaults from Microsoft Learn.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Optional local development: the gateway image and port/connection guidance (gateway listens on port 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to run a local DocumentDB gateway for integration tests.
tools.workaround: Run against the live cluster; follow run-environment instructions to keep secrets out of code.

tools.name: azd, bicep, terraform
tools.needed_for: Not required for the sample (do not provision another cluster per run policy), but normally helpful for infra-as-code or deploying support resources.
tools.detail: azd, bicep, terraform not on PATH (inventory).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot generate or deploy IaC locally from this machine without installing them; not blocking for the sample because the run environment provides an existing cluster.
tools.workaround: Use the existing cluster and the documentdb MCP server; if infra-as-code is later required, install the missing CLI tools.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity checks, interactive verification of indexes and data, local troubleshooting during development.
tools.impact_if_missing: No direct interactive Mongo shell; increases friction when manually verifying connection strings, inspecting documents and indexes.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_get_statistics, etc.) or Azure Portal connection strings / 'Quick start' features to get sample connection strings.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (Quickstart)

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — not installed; would speed sample creation with templates and examples.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource)...
confusions.grounded_answer: The managed MongoDB clusters are deployed using the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (provider Microsoft.DocumentDB).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Old Cosmos DB docs and legacy Cosmos 'databaseAccounts' resource use the same provider namespace; older Mongo-compatible Cosmos DB (RU) used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. The new vCore offering exposes a distinct resource type 'mongoClusters', which many older examples don't show.
confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep/Terraform to create a vCore-managed cluster will either deploy the wrong resource (Cosmos account) or fail for the intended vCore cluster. That would break automation and tests that expect the mongoClusters resource.
improvements: Add a prominent note on the 'databaseAccounts' and 'mongoclusters' Learn pages clarifying that vCore-managed Mongo clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and not databaseAccounts.
Update quickstarts (Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster) to show the exact resource type and an explicit example Bicep/ARM that uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the az cosmosdb command group in the core Azure CLI...
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb mongocluster command group (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create, az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings). There is also a related az cosmosdb mongocluster alias in some CLI distributions, but the authoritative command documented is az documentdb mongocluster.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (Microsoft Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Legacy and alternative CLI command groups (az cosmosdb) are historically used for Cosmos DB accounts; some docs and CLI extensions expose overlapping command names, causing ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster (Azure CLI docs showing similar command)

confusions.build_risk: Running az cosmosdb create (targeting databaseAccounts) could create a different resource type; scripts that use the wrong CLI group may fail or target the wrong API surface.
improvements: Clarify in the CLI docs and quickstarts that az documentdb mongocluster is the documented command group for the vCore-managed DocumentDB Mongo clusters.
Add a short note in 'az cosmosdb' pages linking to the 'az documentdb' CLI group to avoid accidental use.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore-managed MongoDB offering uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in Bicep/ARM (and corresponding Terraform/AzAPI module examples). Do not assume databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the vCore mongoClusters resource.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API and many example templates use databaseAccounts; the new vCore offering introduced a dedicated resource type 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (older ARM docs for Cosmos DB)

confusions.build_risk: Using the databaseAccounts resource in IaC will not create the intended vCore mongoClusters resource; deployment templates would be invalid for the new cluster type.
improvements: Add a clear code-sample section on the 'mongoClusters' Learn page with Bicep and Terraform examples for the common scenarios used by sample apps.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical connection string (Mongo-compatible Cosmos/DocumentDB style): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account-name>@ ...
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB mongoClusters use Mongo-style connection strings often with the SRV scheme and the cluster host suffix (e.g., mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster-name>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000). The docs recommend mongodb+srv and TLS and show authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 or OIDC parameters for Entra ID flows; the old port 10255 pattern is a Cosmos DB SQL-era credential style and is not the canonical value for the vCore mongoClusters cluster.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (connection string examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API examples and some blog posts show a non-SRV connection string using .mongo.cosmos.azure.com with fixed TLS port 10255; newer vCore clusters use SRV endpoints and the mongocluster host suffix and may prefer SCRAM-SHA-256 and SRV scheme.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB-style connection string examples referencing port 10255

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix, port or missing TLS/authMechanism options will cause client drivers to fail to authenticate or to show warnings ('Non-Genuine MongoDB Detected').
improvements: Update quickstarts and sample READMEs used by the agent kit to show the canonical SRV-style connection string for mongoClusters and a clear example for SCRAM-SHA-256 and OIDC/Entra ID connections.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as provisioned compute capacity ... expect vCore/instance-size billing (M30, M40, etc.) and/or a serverless option depending on SKU.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore Mongo offering) is billed by compute-tier (named M-series tiers mapping to vCores + memory) and storage; it is not billed by Request Units (RUs). The correct model is per-shard compute tiers (Mxx) + provisioned storage. Serverless/RU models apply to other Cosmos DB NoSQL/SQL API offerings, not to the vCore DocumentDB clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Cosmos DB family historically uses RUs; the vCore Mongo offering is intentionally a different billing model (compute tiers + storage). Mixing the two models is a common mistake because both live under the broader Cosmos/DocumentDB naming history.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB (RU) pricing docs (example of RU model)

confusions.build_risk: Choosing wrong performance/tiers during sample testing or expecting RU commands or autoscale behavior will cause incorrect expectations about costs and scaling capabilities.
improvements: Add a short 'Billing model' section on the quickstart and overview pages that contrasts vCore (DocumentDB) vs RU/serverless (Cosmos DB for NoSQL), with a sample cost comparison.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported authentication: standard MongoDB auth (SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256) and X.509 ... Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) integration is not universally supported ... token-as-password pattern ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native username/password (SCRAM-SHA-256) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane authentication. For Entra ID you use an OIDC flow: the connection string uses authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC (or MONGODB-OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC-like property in clients) and authMechanismProperties such as TOKEN_RESOURCE and ENVIRONMENT:azure; tooling examples (VS Code extension, MongoDB Compass, mongosh) demonstrate using mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and companion authMechanismProperties. The driver integration is via OIDC/OAuth flows rather than a generic token-as-password simple pattern.

grounding_links.title: Connect using Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflates a variety of token-presentation techniques and suggested a generic 'token-as-password' approach; current DocumentDB guidance prescribes OIDC-style authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and driver-specific OIDC configuration.

confusion_sources.title: Older blog posts / generic OIDC patterns that mention token-as-password

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to implement Entra authentication by simply passing an AccessToken as the password without the proper authMechanism and authMechanismProperties, drivers will reject the connection or authentication won't be authorized.
improvements: Add a short example snippet for Motor/PyMongo showing how to use OIDC (or documented design pattern) in the 'how-to-connect' page.
Document the recommended authMechanism value (MONGODB-OIDC) and the required authMechanismProperties in a small code sample per major language.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers for the language (pymongo / motor for Python...).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo/Motor for Python). For async Python ODM the sample's choice — Motor + Beanie — is appropriate and recommended for async FastAPI apps.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver (examples)

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: HNSW, IVF, DiskANN and an approximate createIndex spec using a 'vector' type...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes exposed via the service search subsystem (cosmosSearch) with sub-types such as vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, and vector-ivf; index creation and tuning are done via the DocumentDB 'createSearchIndexes' / cosmosSearch construct rather than a vanilla createIndex vector spec. Use the documentdb-vector-search guidance for the exact index definitions and tuning parameters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic Mongo-style vector index syntax (some community projects) and didn't reference the service's cosmosSearch/createSearchIndexes semantics. Different managed services expose different vector index APIs.

confusion_sources.title: Generic MongoDB vector index examples (varied community syntaxes)

confusions.build_risk: Using a wrong index creation command will fail or create a non-vector index. This would break any vector-based query/semantic features added to the sample.
improvements: Add a short example 'createSearchIndexes' snippet for vector-diskann on the 'vector-search' Learn page and a one-line example in the agent skill templates.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes or external engine; use Atlas $search if available and merge results client-side.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes integrated full-text and hybrid search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25 scoring) and supports hybrid BM25 + vector search patterns. The recommended surface is createSearchIndexes + $search, not the community $text operator.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB-centric docs point to text indexes or Atlas Search; DocumentDB uses its own createSearchIndexes + $search surface with BM25 and hybrid patterns.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB community text indexes docs and Atlas Search docs

confusions.build_risk: Implementing text search with community text indexes will produce a less featured search experience and deviate from DocumentDB's recommended fast-path $search indexes; sample features around fuzzy or hybrid retrieval could be wrong or underperforming.
improvements: Show a minimal createSearchIndexes + $search example in the sample README to steer builders away from $text.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect support for MongoDB 6.0 or 7.0 wire protocol; many core features supported but some advanced features may be restricted.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports a wide range of MongoDB wire protocol versions (official docs list support for 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0) and claims ~99% operator compatibility. The compatibility docs enumerate supported operators and also list server/diagnostic/admin commands that may be restricted in a PaaS environment. Consult the compatibility matrix on Microsoft Learn for precise feature-level guidance.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged generically and suggested some features might be missing without checking the compatibility matrix. The service publishes a detailed compatibility chart that should be used instead of a broad guess.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a feature is unsupported (or supported) without checking the compatibility table could make the sample inadvertently use an unsupported operator or rely on an unavailable admin command.
improvements: Add a short pointer in sample README to the compatibility matrix with examples of operations the sample must avoid or test for (e.g., admin-only commands).

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator ... use official MongoDB Community Docker image on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is a DocumentDB Gateway Docker image intended for local development: ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local (gateway) exposing Mongo protocol on port 10260 (TLS + SCRAM-SHA-256). The skill 'documentdb-local-deployment' documents using the Gateway image and port 10260 for local parity.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed no service-specific local gateway exists and suggested using the generic mongo image. In fact the DocumentDB project provides a gateway image to improve local parity with the managed service.

confusion_sources.title: Generic advice to run mongo:7.0 locally (community image)

confusions.build_risk: Using plain mongo:7.0 as a local stand-in may not reproduce DocumentDB-specific features or port/connection/TLS behavior (the gateway uses port 10260 and includes TLS/ SCRAM guidance). Tests might pass locally but fail against the managed cluster, or vice versa.
improvements: Add a short 'Local dev' section in the sample README that shows how to run the DocumentDB gateway container (image and port 10260) and how to toggle SKIP_INIT_DATA/INIT_DATA_PATH for seed scripts.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported only if the service exposes a replica-set oplog or equivalent change feed; may be limited for Cosmos compatibility layers.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports change streams (the $changeStream stage / collection.watch) across supported protocol versions; the compatibility docs list $changeStream among supported aggregation pipeline stages. Use the compatibility matrix and test using collection.watch() to confirm on the target cluster.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Some Cosmos DB variants had more restrictive change-feed semantics; the cold answer conservatively hedged that change streams might not be available without checking the compatibility table.
confusions.build_risk: Relying on change streams without verifying on the specific cluster might lead to runtime failures or missing events; the sample should test change stream capability during verification.
improvements: Add a sample 'verify change stream' quick test in the sample's verification scripts that gracefully degrades if not supported.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile (documentdb MCP) for data-plane inspection ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server is the data-plane tool in the inventory and it provides collection/index/plan inspection and mutation tools. The general 'azure' MCP server exists for control-plane tasks but documentdb MCP provides the service-specific data-plane tools.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb (MCP server) as shown in inventory

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically ... Azure DocumentDB became Azure Cosmos DB ... The managed Mongo-compatible offering is either a Mongo API on Cosmos or a separate managed MongoDB cluster; terminology varies.
confusions.grounded_answer: Microsoft renamed the vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB offering to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)'; it is distinct from the original 'DocumentDB' product that became Azure Cosmos DB in 2017 and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB. The new Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine; Cosmos DB (RU/noSQL) and Azure DocumentDB (vCore) are separate offerings.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple renames and overlapping names (DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB, then vCore Mongo branded as Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore), then renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB') cause a lot of naming confusion in older docs and blog posts.

confusion_sources.title: Older blog posts and docs that still reference 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong product name in README or provisioning scripts could mislead users to try to create the other service (Cosmos DB RU) and create incompatibilities.
improvements: Add a brief 'Naming note' at the top of the Learn landing page and the agent kit README clarifying the lineage and the differences between Azure DocumentDB (vCore), Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU), the old DocumentDB->Cosmos rename, and Amazon DocumentDB.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: If the account is Cosmos DB Mongo API, the underlying engine is Cosmos DB’s proprietary store ... If the offering is a managed MongoDB cluster (DocumentDB managed Mongo), the underlying engine is upstream MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore Mongo offering) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol compatibility — it is not upstream MongoDB's server binary. For application code the practical guidance is: use standard MongoDB drivers, but verify feature-level compatibility in the documented compatibility matrix. Do not assume internal engine is upstream MongoDB.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB with Amazon DocumentDB — engine & compatibility details

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the legacy Cosmos Mongo API implementation and general managed-Mongo-hosting assumptions. The service's documentation explicitly states it runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine rather than upstream MongoDB server, which has implications for some admin commands and behaviors.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the engine is upstream MongoDB could lead to using admin or diagnostic commands that are unsupported or relying on internal behaviors not present in DocumentDB.
improvements: State explicitly in quickstarts and the sample README: 'Azure DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine; use standard MongoDB drivers and consult the compatibility matrix for operator-level differences.'

confusions.question: Which database name will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will use the database named sample_customer_360_11 for all created collections and indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment for this sample specifies database sample_customer_360_11.

confusions.question: What environment variable contains the cluster connection string for this run?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Do not hard-code it into files or logs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the sample run-environment requires DOCUMENTDB_URI and instructs not to commit credentials.

confusions.question: Which Python client libraries and install command will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Motor (async pymongo) + Beanie ODM + FastAPI. Install with pip: pip install fastapi uvicorn beanie motor pydantic python-dotenv.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Motor + Beanie + FastAPI is the right async stack. The documentdb-driver skill recommends using a process-wide singleton MongoClient (Motor client) and Beanie.init_beanie to wire models; the pip install list is a reasonable minimal set (pin versions in requirements.txt for reproducibility).
improvements: Pin tested package versions in requirements.txt and add a note in the README about versions used in CI/dev to reduce future breakage.

confusions.question: What TTL index definitions will the sample create to enforce retention?
confusions.cold_answer: Create TTL indexes on the documents using a datetime field (e.g. expireAt) with expireAfterSeconds=0. Example in PyMongo/Beanie: await collection.create_index([('expireAt', 1)], expireAfterSeconds=0). Use expireAt populated to now + retention period when creating consent records.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: create a TTL index on a datetime field and use expireAfterSeconds=0 to implement expireAt semantics; populate the document field with the absolute expiry datetime (now + retention) on write.

confusions.question: What document schema and indexing pattern will the sample use for consent records?
confusions.cold_answer: Consent document schema (Pydantic/Beanie model): customerId, consentVersion, currentPreferences, history array, createdAt/updatedAt/expireAt; index customerId and TTL on expireAt.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a sensible schema and aligns with documentdb-data-modeling guidance: use a Consent document with customerId (indexed), consentVersion, currentPreferences, append-only history array for audit, and an expireAt (or retention_expires_at) datetime for TTL index. Keep history bounded or shard/partition for larger workloads to avoid document-size issues.
improvements: Add a short note in the sample README about the 16 MB document limit and when to move history into a separate collection to avoid large-document issues.

information_gaps.title: Exact package versions to pin
information_gaps.description: Which exact versions of FastAPI, Beanie, Motor, and PyMongo the sample should pin to for tested compatibility with Python 3.13 in this environment. I checked the documentdb-driver and run-environment skills but they do not contain a tested pinned requirements.txt for this sample.

information_gaps.title: Retention period policy
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks to 'Add TTL indexes for data retention enforcement' but does not specify a default retention window (e.g., 365 days). The documentation and skills explain how to implement TTL but do not pick a sensible default for consent records; the builder must choose and document it.

information_gaps.title: Exact request/response JSON shapes & route names
information_gaps.description: The prompt leaves endpoint paths and payload shapes undefined; the builder must decide bodies for record/withdraw endpoints (actor, reason, channels shape). I looked through the installed skills and quickstarts and found no sample JSON shapes to reuse.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create and target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resources and use the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb) when writing IaC or CLI snippets; see the mongoClusters ARM docs for examples.

Use the SRV-style connection string and TLS with authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 (or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID flows). Do not rely on older Cosmos DB port 10255 examples — follow the 'how-to-connect' quickstarts for the correct parameters.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (connection string examples)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Implement Motor + Beanie with a singleton Motor client (create one AsyncIOMotorClient on startup, pass the database to Beanie.init_beanie) and pin dependency versions in requirements.txt.
Create a TTL index on a datetime field (expireAt / retention_expires_at) with expireAfterSeconds=0 and populate it with now + retention_period on writes to implement expireAt semantics.
